title: Ankara Turns to Russia for Fertilizer as Hormuz Closure Bites; Saudi Arabia Eyes KAAN Fighter
subhead: Turkey is set to sign a fertilizer import deal with Russia after the Strait of Hormuz closure cut Gulf supply, while Saudi Arabia joins Egypt in exploring Ankara's fifth-generation KAAN fighter jet as US and Israeli concerns delay Riyadh's F-35 ambitions.

sections.heading: Economy: Ankara Turns to Russia for Fertilizer After Hormuz Closure
sections.body:
Turkey is set to sign a deal with Russia to boost fertilizer imports, according to Bloomberg, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has cut off Gulf supply routes. Turkish Minute reports Ankara is seeking the Russian arrangement specifically because of Gulf supply disruptions, and Türkiye Today frames it as Ankara turning to Moscow 'after Hormuz closure cuts Gulf supply.' The move comes as the ongoing US-Iran confrontation has kept Hormuz transit depressed, forcing importers to scramble for alternative sources.

AgroLatam notes the Russia-Turkey fertilizer deal is putting US farm input costs back in focus, underscoring how the Hormuz disruption is rippling through global agricultural supply chains. For Turkey, a major fertilizer importer, securing Russian supply is a pragmatic hedge against a choke point that remains closed or unreliable.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal shows the Hormuz crisis is now reshaping Turkey's import geography — deepening economic dependence on Russia at a moment when Ankara is also courting Western defense partners, a tension that will be hard to balance.

sections.heading: Defense: Saudi Arabia Joins Egypt in Exploring KAAN as F-35 Ambitions Stall
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia has joined Egypt in exploring Turkey's fifth-generation KAAN fighter jet programme, Business Insider Africa reports, as US and Israeli concerns delay Riyadh's F-35 ambitions. The outlet describes Saudi Arabia as the Middle East's fourth-strongest military now eyeing the Turkish jet. Separately, MiGFlug reports Turkey's Kaan P1 stealth fighter has begun taxi trials, a step toward flight testing.

The development builds on a broader push: The Jerusalem Post and Defence24 report Turkey plans to boost defense spending by 229% over three years in a technology push, a figure that signals how seriously Ankara is investing in indigenous platforms like KAAN as an export alternative to Western systems.
sections.whyItMatters: If Saudi Arabia follows Egypt into the KAAN programme, Turkey's fifth-generation fighter becomes a genuine export competitor to the F-35 in the Gulf — a direct challenge to US defense primacy in the region.

sections.heading: Iraq: Ankara and Baghdad Seek Faster Progress on Development Road
sections.body:
Turkey and Iraq have reaffirmed support to accelerate the Development Road Project, The New Region reports, with Türkiye Today noting both sides want faster progress. Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş said Ankara hopes the project becomes operational soon, according to Middle East Monitor and TRT World. The multi-billion-dollar corridor would link Iraq's Gulf port of Basra to Turkey via rail and road, offering an alternative trade route that bypasses Hormuz.

Kurtulmuş also struck a regional note, telling Daily Sabah that 'peace will prevail in Türkiye, Iraq, beyond' — a comment that ties the infrastructure push to the broader stabilization agenda with Baghdad.
sections.whyItMatters: With Hormuz disrupted, the Development Road's value as a Gulf-to-Europe corridor rises sharply — and Ankara is signaling it wants the project operational sooner rather than later to capture that trade.

sections.heading: Kurdish Peace Process: Qandil Vacuum and the PJAK Question
sections.body:
As the PKK peace process advances, analysts are examining what happens to the group's Qandil stronghold. ACLED argues the peace process is likely to strengthen the PJAK — the PKK's Iranian affiliate — in its confrontation with the Islamic Republic. Amwaj.media asks whether Iranian Kurdish fighters will fill any vacuum left by the PKK in Qandil, while The New Region reports Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces are moving to fill the space left by the PKK in the mountainous border region.

These analyses point to a fluid security situation: as the PKK disarms or withdraws under the peace framework, both Iranian Kurdish groups and Iraqi state-aligned forces are positioning to claim the territory.
sections.whyItMatters: The peace process is not just a Turkish domestic matter — it is reshaping the balance of power in the Qandil mountains, with implications for Iran, Iraq's PMF, and the broader Kurdish landscape.

sections.heading: Domestic Politics: Kılıçdaroğlu Opens Door to İmamoğlu Presidential Bid
sections.body:
CHP leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu has opened the door to a presidential bid by jailed former Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, Euronews reports. The court-appointed CHP leadership has stressed that İmamoğlu is not a 'political prisoner,' according to Daily Sabah and Turkish Minute — a notable framing given the ongoing legal cases against him. The move signals the opposition is positioning İmamoğlu as a potential standard-bearer despite his legal troubles.

This follows the CHP purge and leadership restructuring flagged in recent days, as Kılıçdaroğlu consolidates control and reshapes the party's electoral strategy ahead of the next national vote.
sections.whyItMatters: By keeping İmamoğlu in the presidential picture, the CHP is betting that a jailed, high-profile candidate can galvanize the opposition — a high-risk strategy that depends on his legal situation not deteriorating further.

sections.heading: Domestic: Wind-Fueled Wildfire Forces Evacuations in Antalya
sections.body:
A wind-fueled wildfire has forced hundreds of people from their homes in Turkey, ABC News reports, with firefighters battling the flames. The Caspian Post says the wildfire is spreading in Antalya, a major tourism hub on the Mediterranean coast, as hundreds were evacuated. The blaze adds to a summer of extreme heat and fire risk across the region.

No casualty figures or containment details were immediately available in the reports reviewed.
sections.whyItMatters: A wildfire near Antalya threatens both lives and a key tourism economy at the tail end of the summer season, and tests the government's disaster-response capacity.

bottomLine: Today's developments show Turkey navigating the Hormuz fallout on two fronts: economically, by locking in Russian fertilizer supply to replace disrupted Gulf imports, and strategically, by positioning its KAAN fighter as an F-35 alternative for Gulf buyers like Saudi Arabia and Egypt. Meanwhile, the PKK peace process is redrawing the map in Qandil, the Development Road with Iraq gains urgency as a Hormuz bypass, and the CHP keeps İmamoğlu in the presidential frame. The common thread is a Turkey adapting to a region where Gulf choke points are unreliable and Western defense ties are conditional.
sources: Bloomberg, Turkish Minute, Türkiye Today, AgroLatam, Business Insider Africa, MiGFlug, The Jerusalem Post, Defence24, The New Region, Middle East Monitor, TRT World, Daily Sabah, ACLED, Amwaj.media, Euronews, ABC News, Caspian Post
